o: We may double up to k elements (each at most once) and want to maximize length × GCD over contiguous subarrays. Doubling only ever appends a factor of 2, so a candidate GCD g is achievable in a window iff every element x satisfies g | x (use as-is) or g | 2x (spend one doubling). Example 1: doubling 2→4 makes GCD 4 over length 2 → 8. Example 2: best is a single doubled element 14 → 14. Example 3: nothing beats 3×5=15. With n ≤ 1500 we can afford roughly O(n²) candidate work.
k: A window supports candidate g iff 2·x ≡ 0 (mod g) for every x in it; each failing element costs exactly one doubling.
The optimal GCD always equals gcd(nums[i], 2·nums[j]) for some pair i, j (including i = j), so enumerating all O(n²) pairs generates every useful candidate.
For a fixed g, the cheapest valid window is found with a sliding window tracking how many elements would need doubling.

a.n: Approach 1: Pairwise Candidate GCDs + Sliding Window
a.i: Collect every value gcd(nums[i], 2·nums[j]) over all pairs — the true optimum must be among them. For each candidate g, slide a window counting elements where 2·x % g ≠ 0 (unusable even with doubling); shrink while that count exceeds k, and record (window length) × g.
s: Build the set of candidates gcd(nums[i], 2·nums[j]) for all i, j.
For each g, sweep r = 0..n−1 adding cost 1 when 2·nums[r] % g ≠ 0.
Shrink left while cost > k; update answer with (r − l + 1) · g.
a.t: O(n² · log V + C · n) where C is the number of distinct candidates (small in practice) — pair enumeration dominates.

a.n: Approach 2: Incremental GCD-State Map per Left Endpoint
a.i: Fix a left endpoint and extend right, maintaining a map from achievable GCD to the minimum doublings needed. Extending by x transforms each state g into gcd(g, x) (same cost) and gcd(g, 2x) (cost + 1), plus the fresh states x (cost 0) and 2x (cost 1). Only O(log V) distinct GCDs survive per left endpoint, keeping this fast and provably exhaustive.
s: For each l, keep dict states: gcd → min doublings, initially empty.
For each r, build new states by combining old states with nums[r] and 2·nums[r]; drop states with cost > k.
Update the answer with (r − l + 1) · g for every surviving state.
a.t: O(n² · S · log V) where S (distinct GCD states per left endpoint) is O(log V) — comfortably fast for n = 1500.

w: Prefer Approach 1 in an interview — it is shorter and its correctness hinges on one clean claim about candidate GCDs. Pitfall: the usability test must be `2·x % g == 0`, not `x % g == 0` (an element like x=2 supports g=4 only after doubling). Follow-up: what if elements could be doubled multiple times, or operations were global rather than per-window?
